title: Tender Management: Process, Software, Best Practices (2026)
summary: Learn what tender management is, key processes, best practices, and how AI software improves tender handling across industries.
body_text: Winning a high-value tender often feels like a race against the clock. In sectors like healthcare, infrastructure, or government, even a small execution slip can derail months of work, such as missing a mandatory compliance clause, submitting an outdated certification, or waiting too long for legal sign-off and missing the deadline entirely. It isn’t just about having the best solution anymore; it’s about presenting it exactly as the buyer demands, with zero ambiguity and full compliance. In 2026, the stakes are higher for three reasons: tender volumes are increasing, evaluation criteria are becoming more granular, and compliance scrutiny is tightening across regulated industries. Teams are expected to respond faster while coordinating deeper technical, legal, and commercial details across more stakeholders than ever before. The most successful organizations have moved away from last-minute scrambles toward predictable tender management processes that protect both win rates and team bandwidth. This guide explains how tender management works, where execution typically breaks down, and how modern tools help teams move faster without increasing risk or burnout. TL;DR (Key Takeaways) Tender management is an execution discipline, not just documentation. Winning teams focus on process control, compliance, and response quality, not just submission speed. Most tender failures come from poor prioritization and weak internal coordination , not pricing or technical gaps. As tender volume and complexity increase, manual workflows stop scaling , leading to rework, missed requirements, and higher risk. Modern tender management combines structured processes with AI support to reduce rewriting, maintain accuracy, and improve consistency across bids. Teams that treat tender responses as reusable strategic assets , not one-off efforts, achieve higher win rates over time. What Is Tender Management? Tender management is the structured, end-to-end process of planning, preparing, managing, and submitting tenders or bids to secure contracts for goods, services, or projects. It ensures that every submission is complete, compliant, competitive, and aligned with the buyer’s requirements and evaluation criteria. In practical terms, tender management coordinates multiple activities: Identifying suitable tender opportunities Interpreting technical, commercial, and legal requirements Developing a bid strategy and pricing approach Creating, reviewing, and validating response content Managing internal approvals and submission deadlines Capturing feedback for future improvement Tender management acts as the bridge between what an organization can deliver and what a buyer expects to receive. When executed well, it reduces wasted effort, minimizes compliance risk, and improves the quality and consistency of submissions. Over time, this structured approach strengthens an organization’s credibility and increases its likelihood of winning repeat contracts. While the meaning of tender management can vary slightly by region and industry, the core principle remains the same: disciplined control over how tenders are evaluated, prepared, and executed. This guide focuses primarily on bidder-side tender management, covering how organizations respond to tenders, coordinate internal teams, manage compliance, and improve win rates across competitive bidding environments. Tender vs Bid vs Proposal vs RFP: Clearing the Terminology Tender management is often misunderstood because related terms are used interchangeably, even though they represent different parts of the procurement process. Clarifying these distinctions is essential for building a consistent and repeatable tender workflow. Tender A tender is the formal request issued by a buyer inviting suppliers to submit offers. Outside the United States, the term “tender” is often used instead of RFP. It defines the scope, requirements, timelines, and evaluation criteria that suppliers must follow. RFP, RFQ, and ITT These are buyer-issued documents within the tender system: RFP (Request for Proposal): Focuses on solution approach, methodology, and value RFQ (Request for Quotation): Emphasizes pricing for a clearly defined scope ITT (Invitation to Tender): Common in public procurement, particularly in the UK and EU, where formal ITTs are used for regulated government and infrastructure contracts All of these documents serve as inputs into the broader tender management process. Bid A bid is the supplier’s formal response to a tender. It typically includes pricing, technical details, compliance declarations, and supporting documentation required by the buyer. Proposal A proposal is the structured narrative within a bid that explains how the supplier will meet the buyer’s requirements and why they are the best choice. Proposals are often embedded within bids but may also be used independently in certain sales contexts. How Do These Fit Together? Tender management sits at the top as the overarching process. The buyer issues a tender (RFP, RFQ, or ITT), suppliers respond with bids, and those bids contain proposals . Understanding this hierarchy helps teams design clearer workflows and avoid confusion during execution. See how AI fits into a structured tender management workflow Explore how Inventive AI supports requirement analysis, drafting, and compliance across complex tenders. Schedule Your Demo Now. Buyer-Side vs Bidder-Side Tender Management Tender management applies to both sides of the procurement process, but the objectives, risks, and success criteria differ significantly. Understanding this distinction is important because tender workflows, tools, and best practices look very different depending on whether an organization is issuing a tender or responding to one. Buyer-Side Tender Management On the buyer side, tender management focuses on transparency, compliance, and value-for-money. Organizations issuing tenders are responsible for: Defining clear requirements and evaluation criteria Ensuring fair competition and auditability Managing communications with multiple bidders Evaluating submissions objectively and consistently Buyer-side tender management is most common in public procurement, infrastructure, utilities, and other regulated environments where procedural accuracy and defensibility are critical. Bidder-Side Tender Management On the bidder side, tender management is about maximizing win probability while controlling cost, risk, and internal effort. Key priorities include: Selecting the right tender opportunities Producing compliant, high-quality responses Coordinating cross-functional contributors Managing deadlines, reviews, and approvals Most discussions around tender management software, automation, and AI focus on this bidder-side workflow, where execution quality and scalability directly affect win rates. Also read : How to Improve Your RFP Win Rates The Tender Management Process (End-to-End) - 8 Stages The tender management process follows a defined sequence of stages designed to ensure fairness, compliance, and informed decision-making. While the specifics vary by industry and geography, high-performing teams follow a repeatable structure that minimizes risk and improves outcomes. 1. Opportunity Identification and Qualification The process begins with identifying relevant tender opportunities that align with organizational capabilities, capacity, and strategic goals. This step filters out low-probability or misaligned tenders before resources are committed. Key activities include: Monitoring public portals, private invitations, and industry networks Assessing scope, budget, timelines, and eligibility requirements Conducting a go/no-go evaluation based on fit and win probability This stage is critical. Poor qualification decisions are one of the most common causes of wasted tender effort. 2. Requirement Analysis and Interpretation Once an opportunity is qualified, teams analyze the tender documentation in detail. This includes technical specifications, commercial terms, evaluation criteria, and submission instructions. At this stage, cross-functional alignment becomes essential. Sales, operations, legal, finance, and subject-matter experts must agree on: Mandatory vs optional requirements Compliance risks and constraints Areas requiring clarification or assumptions Misinterpreting even a single requirement can lead to disqualification, regardless of proposal quality. Related : Understanding RFQ and RFP Differences Explained 3. Bid Strategy and Positioning A bid strategy defines how the organization will compete and differentiate. This is where tender management shifts from compliance to competitiveness. Key strategic decisions include: Pricing and commercial positioning Differentiators tied to buyer priorities Risk mitigation and delivery approach Strong strategies align closely with the buyer’s evaluation model rather than internal preferences. Teams that treat this stage lightly often produce compliant but uncompetitive bids. 4. Content Development and Drafting Content creation is the most visible part of tender management, but it should not be the starting point. By this stage, requirements and strategy should already be clear. Core components typically include: Executive summary and value narrative Technical response and methodology Commercial and pricing sections Compliance matrices and supporting documents High-performing teams reuse structured knowledge while tailoring responses to the specific tender context, avoiding generic language. 5. Review, Approval, and Quality Control Before submission, bids go through multiple layers of review. This includes: Technical accuracy checks Legal and compliance validation Financial consistency and pricing review Editorial review for clarity and tone A structured review process reduces last-minute changes and prevents avoidable errors. 6. Submission and Confirmation Tender submissions are time-bound and procedural. Teams must ensure: Correct formats and portals are used All mandatory documents are included Submission receipts or confirmations are captured Late or incomplete submissions are typically rejected automatically, regardless of content quality. 7. Post-Submission Clarifications and Follow-Up After submission, buyers may request clarifications or additional information. Prompt, consistent responses signal professionalism and reliability. Maintaining structured communication during this phase can influence final evaluations, especially in competitive or negotiated tenders. 8. Outcome Review and Continuous Improvement Whether successful or not, every tender should be reviewed. Feedback, scoring insights, and internal observations should be documented and stored centrally. This learning loop strengthens future tender performance and prevents repeat mistakes. Also read : How to Create an Effective RFP Response Guide Common Challenges in Tender Management Despite having structured processes, many organizations struggle to execute tender management effectively at scale. As procurement becomes more centralized and tendering expands across regions and product lines, teams are handling more concurrent tenders than ever before. Each submission now demands deeper compliance checks, more cross-functional input, and tighter timelines. Without scalable workflows, this increase in volume quickly overwhelms manual coordination, leading to rushed reviews, duplicated effort, and a higher risk of errors. ‍ 1. Managing Complexity and Volume Modern tenders are longer, more detailed, and more frequent. Teams often handle multiple live tenders simultaneously, each with different requirements and deadlines. Without a centralized system, information fragmentation becomes unavoidable. 2. Tight Deadlines and Resource Pressure Tender timelines are non-negotiable. Late submissions or rushed reviews are among the most common reasons bids fail. Small and mid-sized teams are particularly vulnerable when relying on manual coordination and spreadsheets. 3. Inconsistent or Outdated Content Reusing past answers without proper validation introduces risk. Inconsistent product descriptions, outdated certifications, or conflicting security responses can undermine trust with evaluators. 4. Cross-Functional Collaboration Gaps Tender responses require input from sales, legal, finance, security, and delivery teams. Without clear ownership and visibility, approvals become bottlenecks and accountability breaks down. 5. Compliance and Regulatory Risk Many tenders impose mandatory compliance thresholds. Missing a single declaration or misinterpreting a requirement can result in automatic rejection, regardless of solution quality. 6. Limited Feedback Loops Organizations often fail to systematically capture feedback from lost tenders. Without structured post-mortems, the same mistakes are repeated across future bids. Also read : RFP Content Management Best Practices and Tips Industries Where Tender Management Is Critical Tender management is not industry-specific, but its importance increases sharply in sectors where contracts are high-value, compliance-heavy, and publicly scrutinized. In these environments, a weak tender process directly translates into lost revenue or regulatory risk. 1. Construction and Infrastructure Construction and infrastructure projects rely heavily on formal tenders, particularly in public-sector and large private developments. These tenders typically involve: Detailed technical specifications Multi-year delivery timelines Strict regulatory and safety requirements Complex pricing and subcontractor structures Effective tender management ensures that cost estimates, timelines, compliance documents, and technical narratives remain consistent across large bid teams. Poor coordination or outdated information is a common cause of disqualification in this sector. 2. Healthcare and Life Sciences Healthcare tenders often cover medical equipment, pharmaceuticals, hospital services, digital health platforms, and public health initiatives. These tenders are uniquely demanding due to: Regulatory and compliance obligations Data privacy and security requirements Clinical validation and documentation Tender management in healthcare must prioritize accuracy and traceability. Even small inconsistencies in regulatory responses or certifications can invalidate an otherwise strong bid. 3. Technology and IT Services In technology procurement, tenders are used for software development, cybersecurity, cloud services, and digital transformation programs. These tenders often emphasize: Architecture and integration details Security questionnaires Scalability and support models Tender management helps IT vendors align technical depth with business value, ensuring responses are both accurate and accessible to non-technical evaluators. 4. Education and Public Sector Educational institutions and government bodies rely on structured tender systems to ensure fairness and accountability. Tenders in this sector commonly involve: Infrastructure and facilities Learning platforms and content Staffing and service contracts Tender management here must balance strict compliance with clear communication. Public-sector tenders frequently reject bids for procedural errors rather than solution quality. 5. Energy and Utilities Energy and utilities tenders cover large-scale projects such as renewable energy installations, grid modernization, and long-term service contracts. These tenders require: Detailed risk and safety assessments Environmental and sustainability disclosures Long-term financial and operational planning Strong tender management ensures consistency across highly technical and commercial sections while meeting evolving regulatory standards. Schedule Your Demo Now. Best Practices for Effective Tender Management High-performing organizations treat tender management as a repeatable operating system, not a reactive task. The following practices consistently separate teams that win predictably from those that rely on effort alone. 1. Prioritize the Right Opportunities Not every tender is worth pursuing. Strong teams apply structured go/no-go criteria based on: Strategic fit and delivery capability Commercial viability Competitive positioning and past performance This prevents resource drain and keeps teams focused on winnable opportunities. 2. Standardize Without Over-Templating Standardization improves speed and consistency, but excessive templating leads to generic responses. Best practice is to: Standardize structure and compliance elements Customize value narratives and technical explanations This balance preserves efficiency without sacrificing differentiation. 3. Centralize Knowledge and Content Winning teams maintain a single, governed source of truth for: Past tender responses Certifications and compliance statements Case studies and reference material Because centralization reduces duplication, prevents outdated answers, and shortens response cycles. 4. Enforce Structured Reviews Formal review checkpoints catch errors early. Effective reviews cover: Requirement-by-requirement compliance Financial accuracy and consistency Legal and contractual alignment Narrative clarity and tone Late-stage rewrites are usually a sign of weak upstream planning. 5. Build Feedback Loops Post-tender reviews should be systematic, not ad hoc. Capturing evaluation feedback, internal observations, and scoring patterns enables continuous improvement across future tenders. What Is Tender Management Software (and When You Need It)? Tender management software is designed to support and automate key parts of the tender process, particularly on the bidder side. It becomes essential when manual coordination starts to limit scale, accuracy, or speed. What Tender Management Software Does? At a minimum, modern tender management platforms help teams: Track opportunities, deadlines, and responsibilities Centralize tender documents and response content Coordinate contributors and approvals Maintain compliance and version control More advanced platforms extend into analytics, automation, and AI-assisted drafting. When Manual Processes Stop Scaling? Organizations typically benefit from tender management software when: Tender volume increases beyond a few per quarter Multiple teams contribute to each response Compliance requirements become more complex Rewriting and reworking consume excessive time At this point, spreadsheets and shared folders introduce more risk than control. The Role of AI in Modern Tender Management AI is increasingly used to support tender management by: Analyzing tender requirements quickly Generating first-pass drafts grounded in existing knowledge Flagging inconsistencies, gaps, or outdated responses Reducing manual rewriting effort The key distinction is whether AI simply accelerates drafting or actually improves response readiness and accuracy. title: Asda and Morrisons Pasta Salads Recalled Over Listeria Contamination Risk
summary: Several ready-to-eat pasta products sold by Asda and Morrisons have been recalled because of a potential contamination risk involving Listeria monocytogenes. body_text: Several ready-to-eat pasta products sold by Asda and Morrisons have been recalled because of a potential contamination risk involving Listeria monocytogenes . Customers who have purchased the affected products are being advised not to eat them and to return them to the store for a full refund. The recall was announced after food producer Greencore identified a possible food safety issue. The products affected include two pasta salads sold by Asda and a chicken and bacon pasta product sold by Morrisons. The warning is particularly important for people who may be more vulnerable to serious illness from listeria, including older adults, pregnant women, newborn babies and people with weakened immune systems. Which Asda and Morrisons products are affected? According to the recall information provided by the Food Standards Agency, three products are included in the warning. The affected products are: Asda Cheese & Tomato Pasta Salad , 300g, product code 5063089221990, use-by date 10 August 2026 Asda Nacho Cheese Pasta Salad , 500g, product code 5063717198311, use-by date 9 August 2026 Morrisons Chicken and Bacon Pasta , 300g, product code 5010251790587, use-by date 7 August 2026 Consumers should check the product name, pack size, product code and use-by date carefully. If a product matches the details in the recall notice, customers should not eat it. Instead, the affected product should be returned to the store where it was purchased. Customers are entitled to a full refund, and the recall information states that a receipt is not required. Why have the pasta products been recalled? The products have been recalled because of a possible presence of Listeria monocytogenes , the bacterium responsible for listeriosis. Listeria can contaminate food and, in some circumstances, cause illness after a person consumes contaminated products. While listeriosis is considered uncommon, it can become a serious infection, particularly among certain groups of people. The Food Standards Agency advises consumers not to eat food covered by an official recall. Product recalls are issued as a precautionary food safety measure when there is a potential risk to consumers. Retailers selling the affected products are also expected to display notices explaining the recall and advising customers what action to take. What is listeriosis? Listeriosis is an infection caused by the bacterium Listeria monocytogenes . It is generally associated with contaminated food and can affect people in different ways. For many healthy people, listeriosis may cause relatively mild symptoms or no noticeable symptoms at all. However, the infection can be considerably more serious in vulnerable individuals. According to NHS guidance, possible symptoms can include a high temperature, muscle aches or pain, chills, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Some people may initially mistake these symptoms for flu or another common infection. In rare cases, listeriosis can develop into a serious illness. Complications can include meningitis and other severe infections. Because symptoms can vary from person to person, anyone who feels unwell after eating a recalled product should consider seeking appropriate medical advice, particularly if they belong to a higher-risk group. Who is most vulnerable to listeria? Although anyone can potentially become infected with listeria, certain people have a greater risk of developing serious complications. These groups include: People aged 65 and over Pregnant women and their unborn babies Babies under one month old People with weakened immune systems Pregnancy is an especially important consideration because listeriosis can affect both the mother and unborn baby. Anyone who is pregnant and concerned about possible exposure to a recalled food should seek advice from an appropriate healthcare professional. Older adults and people with compromised immune systems should also take food recalls seriously because they may be more likely to develop severe complications. What should you do if you bought a recalled pasta salad? If you have one of the affected products at home, the safest action is simple: do not eat it . Check the packaging against the product details in the recall notice. Pay particular attention to the use-by date and product code, as similar products may not necessarily be included in the recall. If your product matches the recall information, return it to the relevant supermarket for a refund. According to the recall notice, customers do not need to provide a receipt. If you have already eaten an affected product, there is no need to assume that you will become ill. Listeriosis is rare, and exposure does not automatically mean infection will occur. However, anyone who develops symptoms or has concerns should seek medical advice. People in higher-risk groups should be particularly attentive to symptoms following possible exposure. Why are chilled ready-to-eat foods monitored closely? Listeria can contaminate a wide variety of foods. The NHS notes that infections are commonly associated with chilled, ready-to-eat products. Examples can include cold cooked meats, cured meats, smoked or cured fish, cooked shellfish, certain soft and blue cheeses, pâté, prepared sandwiches and salads, pre-cut fruit and products made using unpasteurised milk. One reason food safety authorities pay close attention to these products is that some ready-to-eat foods may be stored in refrigerators for extended periods before being consumed. Following storage instructions and respecting use-by dates are therefore important parts of food safety. Consumers should always follow the storage and preparation instructions printed on food packaging. What does the recall mean for Asda and Morrisons customers? The recall does not mean that all pasta salads or chilled products sold by Asda and Morrisons are unsafe. It specifically concerns the products and identifying details listed in the recall notice. Customers should therefore avoid making assumptions based solely on the brand or product category. Instead, they should check the exact product name, pack size, product code and use-by date. If the details match those included in the recall, the product should not be consumed. Food recalls are an important part of the UK's food safety system. They allow potentially affected products to be removed from sale and enable consumers who have already purchased them to take appropriate action. Key takeaway for shoppers The important message for anyone who has recently purchased one of the affected pasta products is to check the packaging before eating it . The recalled items are the Asda Cheese & Tomato Pasta Salad, Asda Nacho Cheese Pasta Salad and Morrisons Chicken and Bacon Pasta with the specific product codes and use-by dates listed above. If you have a matching product, do not eat it. Return it to the appropriate supermarket for a refund, even if you no longer have your receipt. Anyone who develops symptoms associated with listeriosis should seek medical advice. People who are pregnant, elderly, very young or immunocompromised should take particular care because listeria infection can be more serious in these groups. Source This article is based on the food recall information reported by The Independent , with health information attributed to the UK Food Standards Agency and NHS guidance .

title: Built for the complexity of education: AI that understands your institution
summary: Part of Microsoft IQ, Work IQ provides Microsoft 365 Copilot and agents with context from the work data, relationships, and workflows. Learn more.
body_text: AI use is already widespread across education. According to Microsoft’s 2026 AI in Education report , 92% of surveyed students and education leaders and 88% of surveyed educators reported using AI for school-related purposes.¹ Experimentation is no longer the question. What comes next is: whether AI can move from individual productivity gains to something an entire institution can rely on, across teaching, learning, research, and operations. 92% of surveyed students and education leaders and 88% of surveyed educators reported using AI for school-related purposes.¹ Microsoft 2026 AI in Education report Read the Microsoft Education AI Toolkit That shift is particularly challenging in education. A single institution may support instruction, assessment, advising, financial aid, research, safety, and IT, each with different systems, records, and access requirements. Add student privacy obligations and academic integrity expectations, and a general-purpose AI experience may lack the context and controls required for institutional use. Closing that gap requires both relevant institutional context and safeguards for how information is accessed and used. Microsoft 365 Education is designed to bring those elements together, helping institutions move from isolated AI experimentation toward practical, governed use. Agentic classroom support Consider what a week actually looks like for an educator. Planning, differentiation, and assessment each live in different places, and none of those systems were designed to talk to one another. The result is repetitive, operational work that piles up between a teacher and their students. This is where agents change the equation. Rather than another tool to open, classroom agents work across the systems an educator already uses, helping streamline planning, differentiation, and assessment as connected work rather than separate tasks. Drafting differentiated versions of a lesson for different reading levels, assembling materials aligned to a unit, and pulling assessment results into a picture of who needs help, become part of one flow. The measure of success isn’t the automation itself. It’s what the automation gives back: time for educators to spend on instruction and with students, which is where their impact is greatest. That’s the promise of AI built for teaching and learning, grounded in real instructional workflows rather than generic productivity. Connecting the student experience Fragmented information can also create challenges across the student journey. A student navigating advising, financial aid, accessibility services, and academic support may need to repeat information across several offices. Each additional handoff can add friction at a point when timely, coordinated support matters. With shared context across student services, support can feel more connected throughout the student journey. Students encounter fewer handoffs and receive help that reflects where they are, from orientation to moments when they may need additional support to continue their studies. Behind the scenes, staff have the context to coordinate a more timely response, helping the institution reduce administrative friction while better supporting each student. The outcome institutions are after here isn’t operational efficiency alone. The broader objective is to reduce administrative friction and help staff provide more coordinated, timely support throughout the student journey. The foundation: Intelligence, governance, and trust A capable AI model is only one part of an institution-ready experience. Relevant context, governance, and clearly defined human oversight also matter. Intelligence provides relevant context for AI experiences. Microsoft IQ is the intelligence layer across Microsoft’s AI capabilities, and Work IQ draws on the Microsoft 365 data, relationships, and workflows a user is permitted to access. This context can help Microsoft 365 Copilot and agents surface relevant information from sources such as files, email, messages, and meetings within the institution’s Microsoft 365 environment. Governance comes from the Microsoft 365 platform your institution already administers: identity, permissions, compliance, and data protection, applied consistently to Copilot and to agents. The institutional knowledge this intelligence draws on is your data. It stays yours, under your control and governance. Trust is what makes the first two usable in a school. Microsoft 365 permissions and governance controls help limit access to information a user is authorized to use. Institutions should configure, monitor, and review Copilot and agent experiences in accordance with their privacy, security, and academic-integrity requirements. Together these deliver what education asks of AI: that it be built for teaching and learning, that it work in the flow of education rather than in a separate destination, and that it provide a trusted academic experience institutions can stand behind. Matching capability to readiness Institutions begin from different levels of AI readiness. Microsoft 365 Education offers several ways to get started and expand use over time, based on an institution’s priorities, licensing, governance, and technical readiness. Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat is included in Microsoft 365 and is where many institutions begin, offering educators and staff a secure, everyday AI experience. Microsoft 365 Copilot provides a richer, more relevant experience by bringing AI into the Microsoft 365 apps where teaching, learning, research, and operations already happen. It also enables institutions to delegate multi-step work to agents, choosing the capabilities that best fit their needs and readiness. That progression matters because it lets institutions invest where capability is needed most, adding as governance and readiness mature rather than committing everywhere at once. There’s a similar logic behind how we approach models. Model choice is another consideration. In supported Microsoft 365 Copilot experiences, organizations may have access to different models for different types of work, subject to availability and administrator controls. The more useful question is not simply which model is newest, but which supported experience best fits the task, the institution’s requirements, and the applicable data-processing terms. Where to start None of this requires a large rollout to begin. Start with what’s already in place . Copilot Chat is included in Microsoft 365, which means most institutions already have a secure place to begin. Pick one workflow . Choose a single sequence where the cost is visible such as an educator’s planning time, a student handoff that loses momentum, or an administrative process that consumes staff effort, and start there rather than everywhere. Let governance grow with usage . Expand capability as your controls and confidence mature, rather than committing across the institution at once. Education’s complexity is not something to design around. It is the reality AI must be designed for. Microsoft is focused on bringing together relevant context, institutional controls, and flexible ways to begin, so schools can explore AI on terms that reflect their needs and responsibilities. title: SaaS Discovery: 6 Methods to Find Shadow IT in Google Workspace
summary: Learn how to find shadow IT in Google Workspace with six SaaS discovery methods, from OAuth log audits to email scanning.
body_text: There’s no denying the impact SaaS services have had on businesses. It’s no surprise that 70% of software used by companies today are SaaS applications. For many modern-day startups, that number is 100%. But, even with all their upsides, the rapid adoption of new apps without a proper SaaS management strategy can lead to increased security risks, compliance gaps, and unnecessary costs. SaaS Discovery is the first and most crucial step in SaaS management. Why? You can’t take any decisive action without a complete inventory of all the SaaS apps linked to your business. How else will you know the marketing department has started using a tool to collect the email of website visitors? They don't know anything about GDPR or the other regulations that require user consent. Follow along as we explore: The key benefits of SaaS discovery 6 different ways to discover SaaS apps and the challenges of each method How to leverage automation for effective SaaS discovery Why Shadow IT SaaS discovery is important Every business unit has something to gain from having complete visibility into your SaaS environment. Overall, it helps strengthen the business’s security posture, simplify compliance, save on costs, and improve business efficiency. Gartner projects that by 2027 , 75% of employees will acquire or create technology outside IT's visibility, up from 41% in 2022. With AI-driven tools entering the workplace at an unprecedented pace, organizations risk exposure to compliance failures and data breaches if they fail to maintain oversight. SaaS discovery ensures that both IT and business leaders can anticipate risks before they escalate into larger security or compliance incidents. More specifically, SaaS discovery will help you: Discover shadow IT : You can’t protect what you can’t see. SaaS discovery helps you detect all apps, including those unsanctioned by IT, reducing security risks and compliance violations. Prevent SaaS sprawl : SaaS purchasing is no longer controlled by IT. This decentralized procurement approach leads to tools with overlapping functionalities, causing inefficiencies and wasted spending. Reduce the risk of missed offboarding: When you don’t know which apps a user is using, you can’t completely offboard them. They might retain access to sensitive company data long after they leave the company. Improve workflow planning for IT managers: With complete visibility into the SaaS landscape, IT teams can effectively plan workflows, integrations, and app management strategies that promote efficiency and productivity. Before implementing a formal SaaS discovery process for the B2B marketplace Sary , Khalifah Alsadah noticed "in one instance I found out that a former employee was still using a critical internal system 3 months after he left." 6 Shadow IT SaaS discovery methods you can use: Step-by-step guide Here are six ways you can start identifying the SaaS apps linked to your business domain. You’ll see that each method has its limitations, so you will have to combine multiple ways to get complete visibility. Currently, most organizations no longer rely on a single discovery approach because remote work, flexible procurement, and decentralized teams make SaaS tracking increasingly complex. Instead, businesses combine manual methods with automation to ensure nothing slips through the cracks. That layered approach is now considered a best practice in SaaS governance. 1. Survey Employees This is the simplest and most direct approach. Just ask your employees which apps they’re using. You can send out a survey or request a list of tools employees rely on for their daily tasks. Pros Easy to implement Helps uncover tools that employees acquired without IT knowledge Limitations Employees may forget or overlook certain apps Some may withhold information, especially if they’re using unsanctioned tools Not all employees are aware of what constitutes a SaaS app, leading to incomplete results This SaaS discovery method is a great starting point, but you’ll still need to implement additional methods to get a complete and accurate picture. 2. Audit OAuth logs in Google Workspace Auditing OAuth logs in Google Workspace will help you discover all apps accessed using the “Sign in with Google” option. You’d be surprised how often this happens. OAuth log auditing has become increasingly important as employees adopt AI productivity tools and automation services that often integrate through single sign-on. These connections can pose risks because third-party apps may request broad permissions that go unnoticed without regular audits. Steps: Sign in to the Google Admin Console. Navigate to Security > Access and data control > API controls . Under App Access Control , review the third-party apps that have OAuth access to your domain. Check app permissions to determine if these apps have access to sensitive data. Pros Offers a straightforward way to discover apps without employee involvement Cons Can’t discover apps if employees didn’t use the “Sign in with Google” option Sifting through the log is cumbersome, requiring extensive cleanup, manual vendor-name matching, and ongoing monitoring As with the previous option, relying on this method alone will not give you complete SaaS app visibility. 3. Scan Email Activity for App Invitations This is the holy grail when it comes to SaaS discovery in the modern IT environment. Whenever a user registers for a new SaaS tool, they’re typically sent a confirmation or notification email. By scanning email activity, you can identify these account creation notifications and uncover SaaS apps linked to your business domain. This method is especially valuable in 2026 because most SaaS onboarding flows still rely on email confirmation. With the rise of AI-driven and niche SaaS products entering businesses every month, email activity often provides the earliest and most reliable evidence of adoption. However, scanning requires a balance between thoroughness and respecting user privacy. However, with this method, you’ll need a third-party tool. We’ll explore how AccessOwl simplifies the process, but another option you can use is the Google Apps Manager (GAM) . This is a popular command-line tool that provides an alternative way for Google Workspace admins to manage domain and user settings. Steps: Download and set up GAM. It’s a multiple-step process. Create a script to access the email inbox for all the users and search for keywords such as “welcome,” “confirmation,” or specific SaaS app names. Here’s an example of a simple GAM command to search a user's Gmail inbox for emails containing the word “ChatGPT”. gam user xyz@companyname.com show messages query "ChatGPT" gam user xyz@companyname.com show messages query "ChatGPT" gam user xyz@companyname.com show messages query "ChatGPT" Compile a list of discovered tools based on these email notifications. Pros Provides a nearly foolproof way to detect SaaS app usage Cons Mastering GAM usage takes time Scripting knowledge is required Time and labor-intensive Only works if you know what you are searching for 4. Check Expense Reports Reviewing company expense reports is another excellent way to discover SaaS apps. If you’re specifically tracking apps for SaaS spend management, this method is sufficient in itself. Unfortunately, it doesn't account for free tools, which are still a security and compliance risk. This method is highly relevant in 2026 because the cost of SaaS subscriptions continues to rise and finance teams are under pressure to optimize spend. While it does not catch free apps, it highlights hidden costs like forgotten subscriptions or duplicate licenses that contribute to SaaS sprawl. Steps: Work with your finance department to obtain expense reports. Or look into credit card management tools like Ramp or Brex. Identify recurring payments or subscriptions related to software services. Create a list of apps in use based on the data you collect Pros Excellent for tracking paid SaaS tools for SaaS spend management Cons Doesn’t account for free tools Requires collaboration with finance teams, which could slow down the process 5. Examine Network Activity This was once a popular method to identify SaaS apps but has become less effective as businesses transition to hybrid and remote working models. This method relies on third-party tools like a Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB) to scan network traffic and identify the URLs and services users visit. You’ll then need to translate the data into specific apps that are in use within the business. Nowadays, this method is less reliable because employees often work from home or use personal devices that bypass company-controlled networks. Still, for organizations with centralized office environments or regulated industries where CASB remains a requirement, network analysis can provide useful real-time visibility into SaaS activity. Pros Effective in traditional office environments with a central network Gives real-time data on app usage Cons Less effective in remote/hybrid environments Involves filtering through lots of data 6. Browser Extension You can also use a browser extension that monitors the user's browser window to try and identify instances where they’re logging in to a SaaS app. While this method provides strong visibility, by 2026 employees are increasingly concerned about digital privacy. Many organizations face pushback when rolling out monitoring extensions, especially as regulations around employee tracking tighten. Adoption often depends on creating clear communication about what is being monitored and why. Pros Can help you identify all kinds of SaaS apps regardless of the sign-in method Cons Relies on employee compliance, which can be difficult to enforce Privacy concerns may lead employees to reject the extension Employees can switch to a different browser How to simplify SaaS discovery through automation If you went through the various steps and thought it’s a lot of work, I have good news for you. Automated Shadow IT discovery tools can significantly simplify the process. It eliminates the chances of missing some tools and will save you a lot of time and effort. Manual discovery cannot keep up with the sheer number of apps employees adopt, nor can it scale with global teams working across multiple devices. An automated joiner-mover-leaver flow closes that gap by making discovery part of offboarding instead of a separate chore. The fastest way to see your own shadow IT is a free shadow IT scan from AcessOwl. It leans on Method 2 (Google Workspace or Microsoft OAuth logs) to catch tools in your domain that are set up outside of SSO. Remember, SaaS discovery is an ongoing process. Even after a thorough manual discovery, new apps are regularly added, requiring continuous effort to keep up with the latest tools employees are adopting. This is where SaaS management apps like AccessOwl come in. Why AccessOwl is the best SaaS discovery tool It’s a lightweight, easy-to-use tool that you add on top of Google Workspace for advanced SaaS app management. AccessOwl simplifies SaaS discovery and management by combining the two most effective methods (continuously auditing OAuth logs and scanning email activity). If you want to compare Shadow It discovery tools side by side see our breakdown of the best Shadow IT tools. Now, IT leaders need solutions that deliver continuous visibility without sacrificing employee experience. AccessOwl does exactly that, providing a seamless way to track app usage across distributed teams, personal devices, and cloud environments. By automating discovery and offboarding, it reduces the burden on IT while improving compliance and data protection. It doesn’t matter whether employees are using personal devices, working remotely, or connecting through various networks. AccessOwl gives you full visibility into your organization’s SaaS landscape without the need for manual intervention or scripting expertise. Better yet, it works in the background without interfering with employees’ privacy or productivity. During employee offboarding, AccessOwl will automatically delete a user’s account across all associated SaaS apps (deprovisioning), including those that were unidentified during onboarding. On top of SaaS discovery, AccessOwl helps automate SaaS user access, user account management, and SaaS vendor management, making it the perfect security and compliance partner for IT admins. In short, AccessOwl serves as your single source of truth for all SaaS information, including: SaaS applications linked to your business SaaS users and their associated permissions Vendor information including data location, type of data processed, and compliance status It also comes with a renewal calendar and SaaS cost tracking for effective SaaS spend management. Ready to discover all the SaaS tools used across your organization? Start with our free shadow IT discovery tool and gain full visibility into your environment. FAQ How do I detect shadow IT in Google Workspace? You can start detecting shadow IT by combining four manual methods: survey employees on the tools they use, audit OAuth grants in the Google Admin console, scan mailboxes for signup and confirmation emails, and review expense reports for software charges. Each method has blind spots, use them together. If the manual work gets too time-consuming, a shadow IT discovery tool like AccessOwl automates discovery. How do I stop employees from bypassing Google SSO? You cannot fully prevent it, because any tool can offer email-and-password signup instead. You can reduce it by setting API controls to limit which third-party apps connect, publishing an approved-tools list, and running discovery often so new signups surface quickly. How does shadow IT create offboarding risk? You cannot remove access from a tool you do not know exists. When someone leaves, any app they signed up for outside SSO can keep their account and data active long after their Google account is suspended. How do I detect apps employees signed up for with a username and password If the account never used "Sign in with Google" and never touched your directory, auditing OAuth grants will not surface them. Email scanning is a more reliable method: the signup, welcome, or confirmation email still lands in the user's mailbox no matter how the account was created.
